name: Asprosin

lead: Asprosin is a hormone released from fat tissue during fasting. In mice it tells the liver to release glucose and the brain to increase appetite.
People with obesity or diabetes tend to have higher levels, while people with a rare syndrome of low asprosin are extremely lean. No studies test it for appearance.

paras: It is cleaved from fibrillin-1 by furin. Reported receptors include OLFR734/OR4M1 in the liver and PTPRD in the brain; antibodies against it lowered weight in mouse models.
No approved product exists and no human safety data for administering or blocking it are described in the sources reviewed.

lead: Asprosin is a fasting-induced protein hormone cleaved from fibrillin-1 (encoded by FBN1) and released mainly from white fat. It was described in 2016 by Atul Chopra's group at Baylor College of Medicine as raising blood glucose during fasting, and in 2017 as stimulating appetite through the brain.[1][2][3]

Blood levels of asprosin are reported to be higher in people with obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.[4][5] People with a rare inherited condition that lowers asprosin (marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome) are very lean.[3]
Asprosin is an endogenous hormone. The sources reviewed describe antibody-based approaches that lower it in mice, but no approved product.

paras: The discovery arose from studying two patients with marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome, who had very low plasma asprosin, low insulin and extreme thinness. The 2016 Cell paper described asprosin as a glucogenic hormone acting on the liver, and a 2017 Nature Medicine paper described it as a centrally acting appetite-stimulating hormone.[1][2][3]

OLFR734 was reported as the liver receptor in mice.[6] A 2019 attempt by an industry group to reproduce the glucose effect with recombinant protein was unsuccessful, which its authors attributed to possible reagent problems; later work in 2019 reproduced the effect and named OR4M1 as the receptor, and PTPRD has been reported to mediate the appetite effects.[3]

Studies report higher circulating asprosin in type 2 diabetes and glucose dysregulation, correlated with fasting glucose, triglycerides and insulin resistance.[4][5] Levels have also been reported to differ in obesity, in saliva as well as blood,[7] and to fall after bariatric surgery.[3] These are associations.

No studies found testing asprosin or an asprosin blocker as an appearance treatment in humans. Registered human studies are observational, for example serum asprosin in men with acne vulgaris, and one tracked glucose-dependent asprosin dynamics in 10 people with diabetes.[8][9]

timeline.event: Asprosin described as a fasting-induced glucogenic hormone.[1]
Asprosin described as a centrally acting orexigenic hormone.[2]
OLFR734 reported as liver receptor in mice.[6]
Anti-asprosin antibodies reported to lower glucose, appetite and weight in mouse models.[3]
